analysis.one_liner: Requires better leak detection, remote shutoff valves, and detailed oil spill plans for pipelines, especially around the Great Lakes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, having attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened federal pipeline safety rules. It directed the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration to rewrite oil spill response plans so they specifically cover diluted bitumen — a heavy crude mixed with chemicals that behaves differently in water than ordinary oil — and required companies to publicly report what crude their pipelines carry. It also would have required operators of pipelines in 'high consequence areas' (where a spill would cause the most damage) to install the best available leak-detection and automatic shutoff technology. A companion provision let the safety agency pay its pipeline inspectors more to compete with private-sector salaries, and let NOAA accept outside funding for Great Lakes oil-spill research.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near pipelines and around the Great Lakes, where a spill would threaten drinking water, fisheries, and shorelines for millions of people. Better monitoring and shutoff valves limit how much oil escapes in a leak, and stronger spill plans mean faster, better-informed cleanup. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly if the safety agency can hire and keep the engineers it needs to inspect pipelines and enforce the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Spill response plans would have to name every crude oil carried, including diluted bitumen, describe the water bodies at risk, and show how the operator would detect, contain, and recover oil that sinks in freshwater [S2][S3].

Operators of pipelines in high consequence areas would have been required to implement best available technology for real-time leak monitoring, automatic shutoff, and isolation valves, with a compliance process and limited, justified exemptions [S2][S3].
Operators would have had to publish annual reports on their websites showing what volumes of diluted bitumen and other crudes each pipeline carries and which pipeline sections transport them [S3].
The Transportation Secretary could raise pay for pipeline inspectors and enforcement staff, capped at 30 percent above standard rates, to keep trained engineers at the safety agency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil pipeline operators would bear the cost of installing monitoring and shutoff equipment, preparing more detailed spill plans, and filing risk analyses and public reports. Those costs would partly be passed to shippers and consumers through transport rates, and the inspector pay raises would come from federal (taxpayer) funds.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for operators of pipelines in high consequence areas could be substantial, and some portion would likely reach consumers through shipping rates [S3].

The bill leaves significant discretion to the regulator: operators can get deadline extensions and monitoring waivers if they show compliance is not economically, technically, or operationally feasible, so how much protection materializes depends on agency enforcement [S3].
The 90-day deadline for rewriting the spill-plan rules and the bypass of certain standard rulemaking steps compressed the regulatory process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but targeted: it protects water supplies and shorelines near pipelines, especially the Great Lakes, at a cost mainly to pipeline operators in equipment and reporting. The main weakness is that the safety mandates come with broad waiver authority, so the strength of the protections would have depended heavily on how aggressively the agency used it. It is a modest, sensible safety bill rather than a sweeping one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Gary Peters introduced the bill on May 18, 2022 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action is recorded: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crude oil pipeline operators came out ahead: they avoid the monitoring, shutoff-valve, and public-reporting requirements the bill would have imposed. Ordinary communities near Great Lakes pipelines got no new spill protections.

for.name: Sen. Gary Peters
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PROTECT Our Great Lakes Act and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action in the seven-plus months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have required costly leak-detection and automatic shutoff technology on pipelines in high consequence areas, plus more detailed spill plans and public reporting on what crudes they carry, including diluted bitumen. Its interests ran against the communities whose water those pipelines put at risk.

industries.industry: Pipeline monitoring and valve technology makers
industries.note: The best-available-technology mandate would have created demand for leak detection systems, automatic shutoffs, and remote-control valves. That demand aligns with the public's interest in faster spill detection and shutdown.
